One of the most important things to understand about moral judgments is that they are not like ordinary judgments. If I say that the soup is cold, then I am making a claim about the soup. If you disagree, then you are making a claim about the soup, and we can settle the matter by consulting a thermometer. If I say that the soup is cold, and you say that it is hot, then one of us must be wrong. Moral judgments are not like this. If I say that it is wrong to pollute the environment, and you say that it is not, then we have not disagreed about a matter of fact, like the temperature of the soup. We have disagreed about a value. There is no matter of fact that settles the question of whether it is right or wrong to pollute the environment. If I say that it is wrong to pollute the environment, then I am not making a claim about the environment. I am making a claim about what matters, and what matters in the environment, and what we ought to do as a result of this. If you say that it is not wrong to pollute the environment, then you are not disagreeing with me about the environment. You are disagreeing with me about what matters, and what matters in the environment, and what we ought to do as a result of this. We can settle the matter about the temperature of the soup by consulting a thermometer. But there is no thermometer for morality. If I say that it is wrong to pollute the environment, and you say that it is not, then one of us must be wrong. We cannot both be right, as we could if we disagreed about the temperature of the soup. Moral judgments are not like this. We can both be right, or both be wrong, or one of us can be right and the other wrong. When we make a moral judgment, we are not making a claim about the world that can be settled by consulting the facts. We are making a claim about what matters, and what matters in the world, and what we ought to do as a result of this. If we disagree about morality, then we have not disagreed about the world.
